1.pericope_label: Jehoshaphat, rich and honoured, joined affinity with Ahab by marrying his son to Athaliah; after certain years he went down to Samaria, was feasted with sheep and oxen in abundance, and agreed to go up with Ahab against Ramoth-gilead

schools.summary: Gill has the riches and honour still increasing and makes them the reason Ahab sought friendship and affinity, to which Jehoshaphat agreed, and he reports the Syriac and Arabic reading of two years for the interval before the visit.

Henry divides the king in two, one growing greater by piety and good management and one not growing wiser, calls the marriage the worst match ever made by any of the house of David and offers pride and policy as its motives, reads the feast as a device to wheedle Jehoshaphat into the expedition since the kisses of an enemy are deceitful, and presses the irony that Ramoth and every city of Israel belonged of right to Jehoshaphat as heir of the house of David, so that Ahab was asking help to recover for himself what was never his; he concludes that some men kindnesses are dangerous as well as their society infectious.

Clarke states the affinity plainly, that Athaliah was taken to be wife to Joram, notes that Ramoth-gilead belonged to the Israelites and was then held by the king of Syria, and refers the reader to his fuller notes on the parallel in Kings.

Ellicott finds the phrase about riches and honour repeated word for word from the preceding chapter and reads the prosperity of Judah in the fact that so powerful a monarch sought so intimate a connection, dates the marriage eight or nine years before the visit and the visit to the sixteenth or seventeenth year of the reign, treats the royal hospitality as part of a deliberate plan to obtain co-operation, and glosses the verb rendered persuaded as incited or pricked on, a word used especially of urging to evil; Keil and Delitzsch set this account beside the fuller one in Kings, find them agreed except in the introduction, and observe that the chronicler exchanged the exact date in the third year, intelligible only in the light of the earlier wars, for an indefinite one.

debates.question: How long after the marriage was the visit to Samaria?

sides.position: two years, on the authority of the Syriac and Arabic
the third year, reckoned from the truce between Syria and Israel, which puts the visit in the sixteenth or seventeenth year of the reign

outliers: Keil and Delitzsch alone explain why the chronicler dropped the date, that in the third year means nothing apart from the history of Ahab earlier wars.
Henry alone asks by what right Ahab sought help to recover a city that belonged to Jehoshaphat as heir of the house of David.
themes: riches and honour that bought a bad alliance
a marriage into the house of Ahab
a feast laid as a snare
a city claimed by both kings

4.pericope_label: Jehoshaphat asked for the word of the LORD; Ahab gathered four hundred prophets who promised victory, and when Jehoshaphat asked for another Micaiah was sent for, while the two kings sat enthroned in their robes and Zedekiah made horns of iron

schools.summary: Henry declines to repeat what he wrote on the parallel in Kings and draws reflections instead: the duty of acknowledging God in all our ways and enquiring at his word, an enquiry made by particular believing prayer, by unbiased consultation of the scriptures and our own consciences, and by regard to the hints of providence; the danger of bad company even to good men, since Jehoshaphat in complaisance sits in his robes hearing lies told in the name of the Lord and will rebuke neither the king who hates a prophet nor the false prophet who abuses the faithful seer, and those who venture among the seats of the scornful cannot come off without a great deal of the guilt of omitted duty; and the unhappiness of a man surrounded by flatterers who cry peace, since that counsel is not always best for us which is most pleasing to us.

Wesley gives Henry rule about enquiring back in almost the same words; Clarke quotes the Targum contrast, that Ahab consulted false prophets while Jehoshaphat sought instruction from the presence of the Lord and prayed at the entering in of Samaria, and that before these all the false prophets prophesied lies.

Ellicott marks where the chronicler differs from Kings, the four hundred given flatly rather than about four hundred, the true God for the Lord, the singular shall I go which he thinks obviously more appropriate, and Ahab complaint sharpened to all his days for evil, extending the grievance over the prophet whole career; he derives Micaiah name from an older form meaning who is like Iahu, Iahu being probably the oldest shape of the divine name, and the father name from a root meaning he is full; he hears Jehoshaphat deprecating an omen; he prefers the Syriac reading of the robes, raiment spotted white and black, since the Hebrew lacks the possessive, and takes the void place for a threshingfloor while suspecting the word corrupt and grown out of the term for spotted; he distinguishes the participle used of the court prophets, which also means mad or raving, from the plainer form used later, and traces the root to an Assyrian verb meaning to call or proclaim; and he compares Micaiah first answer, as the chronicler has recast it to name the Syrians outright, with the Delphic oracle about the crossing of the Halys.

outliers: Ellicott alone compares the recast answer with the studied ambiguity of the Delphic oracle.
Clarke alone brings in the Targum picture of Jehoshaphat praying at the entering in of Samaria while the false prophets spoke.
themes: four hundred prophets with one voice
a king who hated the one prophet who told him the truth
two thrones at the gate of Samaria
an oracle framed to be read either way

15.pericope_label: Micaiah foretold Israel scattered as sheep without a shepherd, then told of the LORD on his throne and of the spirit that volunteered to be a lying spirit in the mouth of the prophets; Zedekiah struck him and Ahab sent him to prison on the bread and water of affliction

schools.summary: Henry takes the permission given to the lying spirit as the heart of the passage: one lying spirit can make four hundred lying prophets and use them to deceive a king, so that the devil becomes a murderer by being a liar and destroys men by deceiving them, and there is justice in God giving up to strong delusions those who will not receive the love of the truth but rebel against it; he closes on the hard case of faithful ministers, hated and persecuted and ill-treated for being true to their God and just and kind to the souls of men, with Micaiah buffeted, imprisoned and condemned to prison fare for discharging a good conscience, yet able to appeal with assurance to the issue, as all may who are persecuted for their faithfulness, since the day will declare who was right and who wrong.

Clarke reports the Targum strange gloss that the volunteer was the spirit of Naboth of Jezreel, who came out from the abode of the righteous and offered to be a spirit of false prophecy in the mouth of the prophets, was given the power but told that whoever speaks falsely can have no mansion among the righteous and must go forth and do as he had said; Wesley repeats Henry sayings about the one lying spirit and about the lot of faithful ministers almost word for word.

Ellicott compares Ahab adjuration with the demand the high priest would put to Christ, notes that the chronicler abridged the host of heaven standing on both sides of the throne to the right hand only, reports that the Greek translators read the opening word of the vision as a denial rather than a consequence, and holds the odd dialogue form of the next verse certainly right; he renders a spirit of falsehood rather than a lying spirit and sets beside it the place in Ezekiel where God says of a deceived prophet that he himself deceived him, the verb there being the one rendered entice here; he makes Zedekiah destined rather than merely liable to see the day of hiding in a chamber within a chamber, and follows Ewald in taking the silence about his later history for a sign that the original narrative held much more than the present extract; he reads the prison fare as bread with stint and water with stint, the word meaning literally a squeezing, which the Vulgate turns into a little bread and a very little water and the Syriac into enough of each to keep life; and he observes that Micaiah closing words to the bystanders are the very words that open the book of Micah, where Hitzig makes them a borrowing and Thenius argues instead that the section bears indubitable marks of historical truth and probably comes from the history of Jehoshaphat written by Jehu the son of Hanani.

debates.question: Who was the spirit that volunteered to deceive Ahab?

sides.position: the spirit of Naboth of Jezreel, come out from the abode of the righteous, which Clarke reports from the Targum and calls a strange gloss
an unnamed spirit of falsehood, with the stress laid on the word in Ezekiel where God says he himself deceived the prophet he gave over
the devil, who becomes a murderer by being a liar and destroys men by deceiving them

outliers: Ellicott alone follows Ewald in reading the silence about Zedekiah later history as evidence that the chronicler is quoting a fuller narrative.
Ellicott alone weighs Hitzig against Thenius on whether Micaiah closing words were borrowed from the book of Micah or belong to an older history of Jehoshaphat.
themes: a spirit that volunteered to lie
four hundred mouths and one deceit

28.pericope_label: Both kings went up to Ramoth-gilead; Ahab disguised himself while Jehoshaphat wore his robes, and the Syrian captains, ordered to fight only with the king of Israel, surrounded Jehoshaphat until he cried out and the LORD drew them away from him

schools.summary: Henry suspects that Ahab, while professing friendship, was really aiming at Jehoshaphat life so as to have the management of his own son-in-law the successor, since otherwise he would never have advised him to enter the battle in royal raiment and make himself an easy mark; if that was the design it was as unprincipled a treachery as ever man was guilty of, and Ahab was justly taken in the pit he had dug for his friend, while the unwary prince, vigorously attacked, would have wished himself too late in the habit of the poorest soldier. Henry offers three senses for the cry and draws the conclusion that God has all men hearts in his hand and turns them as he pleases, contrary to their own first intentions, so that many are moved unaccountably both to themselves and others by an invisible power.

Wesley gives Henry three senses of the cry in the same order and adds that it was not in vain, since God moved the captains to depart; Clarke quotes the Targum, that Jehoshaphat cried and the Word of the Lord brought him assistance, and refers to his notes on the parallel in Kings for the disguise.

Ellicott hears Ahab words as a hurried exclamation, disguising myself and entering, and notes that where Kings has Ahab alone go into the battle this account has both kings go, with the Syriac, the Greek, the Vulgate, the Arabic and the Targum agreeing; the thirty-two captains of Kings are left unnumbered here because the chronicler passed over the earlier war they belong to, though the Syriac and Arabic supply the number, and the verb of the encirclement is better rendered came round against him than turned aside against him, the difference in the Hebrew turning on half a letter. Since the Kings account ends at the cry, he holds the clause about the Lord helping him and inciting the captains away to be from the chronicler own pen, and reasons that the chronicler must have taken the cry for a prayer, a sense the verb often bears; the captains discovering their mistake and retiring is a perfectly natural event rightly called providential, since Hebrew faith knows nothing of an order of the world that can be separated even in thought from the constant personal activity of God.

sides.position: left open among three, a call to his friends to relieve him, a call to his enemies to correct their mistake, or a prayer to God
a prayer, since the clause about the Lord helping him is the chronicler own addition and presupposes it
a prayer answered, the Word of the Lord bringing him assistance, as the Targum has it

outliers: Ellicott alone identifies the clause about the Lord helping Jehoshaphat as an addition from the chronicler own pen and reasons from it to the sense of the verb.
Henry alone reads the advice to wear the robes as an attempt on Jehoshaphat life.
themes: a king in disguise and a king in his robes
a mistake in the Syrian ranks
a cry heard in the middle of a battle

33.pericope_label: A man drew a bow at a venture and smote the king of Israel between the joints of the harness; Ahab held himself up in his chariot facing the Syrians until the evening, and died

schools.summary: Henry sets the two kings side by side: wicked Ahab disguising himself, arming himself, as he thought securing himself, and slain all the same, since no art and no arms can save those whom God has appointed to ruin, so that Jehoshaphat is safe in his robes and Ahab killed in his armour, the race not being to the swift nor the battle to the strong.

Clarke prefers the Targum, which names the archer as Naaman, captain of the host of the great king of Syria, drawing a bow that the prophecy of Elijah the Tishbite and of Micaiah the son of Imla might be fulfilled and smiting the king between the heart and the caul of the liver where the coat of mail is joined; he admires the last act of the king of Israel as true personal courage and patriotism, since Ahab knew his troops would give way at once if they found he was mortally wounded and that the slaughter in the pursuit would be great, so that but for the accident the Syrians had probably been defeated; and he closes with a caution the reader should never forget, that God is repeatedly represented in the Bible as doing what, in the course of his providence, he only permits to be done. Wesley puts Henry antithesis of robes and armour in two lines.

Ellicott compares the phrase at a venture with a similar expression elsewhere which Gesenius interprets as without thought of evil design, calls the Greek with good aim a bad guess, reports the Syriac innocently straight before him, and judges the explanation of Rashi best of all, that the archer did not know why he chose that particular man to shoot at; he takes the joints of the harness for the breastplate, with the Syriac reading between the division of his mail, and dismisses the Greek in the midst of the lungs and breast and the Vulgate between the neck and shoulders as mere guesses; he prefers the reading of this book, that the king continued holding himself up in the chariot facing Aram until the evening, to the reading in Kings, because the sense is that Ahab bravely bore up against the pain of his wound in order not to discourage his own side by retiring from the field; and he explains the omission of the return of the army and the washing of the chariot at the pool of Samaria by Jehoshaphat having had no part in it, and perhaps by the chronicler true perception of the real climax of this vivid story of the olden time.

debates.question: Was the arrow aimed at Ahab or not?

sides.position: not aimed: the archer did not know why he chose that particular man to shoot at, which Ellicott judges the best of the explanations offered
aimed, Naaman drawing the bow against him that the prophecies of Elijah and Micaiah might be fulfilled, as the Targum has it

outliers: Clarke alone presses the general caution that Scripture represents God as doing what his providence only permits to be done.
Ellicott alone prefers the reading of this book to that of Kings on the ground of what it implies about Ahab courage.
themes: an arrow shot at a venture
a king propped up in his chariot until evening
a story the chronicler ends at its climax
